context.problemStatement:
Implement the `Lambda` case of `eval`. An anonymous function `fn(x) { ... }`
evaluates to a function value. Nothing in its body is evaluated until it is
called, so this case never returns an error. Build a `VFunc(UserFn(...))` whose
name is `"lambda"` (used in error messages) and whose parent is the environment
in which this function was *defined*, not the one in which it will be called. This
is what lets a function use the names around it, even after the call that created it
has returned.

```
// In eval:
    Lambda(params, body) ->
      // YOUR CODE HERE (replace the code below)
      Error(errors.NotImplemented(
        "Lambda("
        <> string.inspect(params)
        <> ", "
        <> string.inspect(body)
        <> ")",
      ))
```

Run the tests:

```
gleam test -- q8
```

targets.claim: Student can explain why their Lambda case never returns an error even when the body of the anonymous function uses an unbound name, and when such an error would appear instead.

probes.question: In your `Lambda(params, body)` branch, why does evaluating an anonymous function whose `body` contains an unbound variable not return an `Error`, and when would that unbound variable error actually be raised?
probes.reason: Directly assesses why the lambda definition avoids errors despite unbound variables in its body and identifies when that evaluation and error trigger instead.

probes.question: If `body` in `Lambda(params, body)` has an invalid name like `Var("undefined_var")`, why does `eval` still return `Ok(...)` on this line, and at what point in program execution would that invalid name be detected?
probes.reason: Provides a concrete variable example to test the distinction between function creation time and function application time.
